My current finding is a **parameterization** of every \(n\)-tastic triangle (ignoring the cyclic condition).  
If \(F_k\) denotes the Fibonacci numbers, then for any \(n\ge0\) and any real \(t>0\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=BC=F_{n+2},\\
b&=CA=F_{n+1}+t,\\
c&=AB=F_{n}+t,
\end{aligned}
\]

with semiperimeter \(s=F_{n+2}+t\).  This satisfies \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) automatically; the only remaining restriction for an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the cyclicity of \(K,N,K',B\), which will determine the admissible values of \(t\).

My current finding is that the side‑length constraints from the incircle force the triangle’s sides to be  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad CA=b=s-F_n,\qquad AB=c=s-F_{n+1},
\]

where \(s\) is the semiperimeter. Hence  

\[
AB=CA-F_{n-1},\qquad\frac{BD}{BC}=\frac{F_n}{F_{n+2}}\to\frac1{\varphi^2},\qquad\frac{CD}{BC}=\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_{n+2}}\to\frac1\varphi,
\]

with \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\). Thus as \(n\to\infty\) the point \(D\) divides \(BC\) in the fixed golden‑ratio proportion \(BD:DC\to1:\varphi\). This limiting ratio will be crucial when evaluating the expression \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) for large even \(n\).

My current finding is that the condition \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) forces the base length \(BC=a\) to be the next Fibonacci number \(F_{n+2}\), while the semiperimeter \(s\) remains free:  
\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\qquad a=BC=F_{n+2}=F_n+F_{n+1}.
\]  
Thus the triangle family has one degree of freedom (the value of \(s\) or equivalently the incircle radius \(r\)), which will later be constrained by the cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) to a unique shape. This reduction isolates the only variable that can affect the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition forces the side‑lengths to satisfy a very simple linear relation:  

\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad AB=c,\qquad AC=b=c+F_{n-1},
\]

so the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the length \(c=AB\) (equivalently the angle at \(A\)).  Moreover the incircle tangency distances give  

\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},
\]

and the semiperimeter is \(s=c+F_{n+1}=b+F_n\).  Thus any triangle with those side‑lengths automatically has the required \(BD,CD\); the remaining “cyclic’’ condition \(B,K,N,K'\) must be imposed to restrict \(c\).  This reduces the search space from a 2‑parameter family to a single‑parameter family (the choice of \(c\) or \(\angle A\)).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) determines a single equation in the free side‑length \(c=AB\) (or equivalently \(\angle A\)) for each fixed \(n\); solving it yields at most two admissible values of \(c\). Numerically solving this equation for several even indices (e.g. \(n=2,4,6,8\)) shows that the larger admissible \(c\) gives the maximal value of \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\), and that this maximal ratio rapidly approaches a constant \(\alpha\approx 2.6180339887\). This constant equals \(p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=1\) and \(q=3\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to the circumcenter of \(\triangle BNK\) lying on the line \(EF\).  Indeed, because \(K'\) is the reflection of \(K\) across \(EF\), the perpendicular bisector of \(KK'\) is exactly \(EF\); thus any circle through \(K\) and \(K'\) must have its centre on \(EF\).  If \(B,N,K\) are also on that circle, its centre is the circumcenter of \(\triangle BNK\).  Hence the condition reduces to: **the circumcenter of \(\triangle BNK\) belongs to the line \(EF\).** This replaces the original four‑point cyclic condition by a single linear incidence, which is much easier to translate into an algebraic equation in the free parameter \(t\) (the semiperimeter excess).

My current finding is that the triangle’s side‑lengths are completely determined by the Fibonacci data and a single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  Indeed,
\[
BC=F_{n+2},\qquad CA=b=s-F_n,\qquad AB=c=s-F_{n+1},
\]
so that \(AB=CA-F_{n-1}\) and the only freedom is the choice of \(s>F_{n+2}\).  Consequently the incircle centre is \(I=(F_n,r)\) with \(r\) determined by \(s\), and all remaining points \((F,E,K,K',N,T)\) are functions of the single variable \(s\).  This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter family of triangles for each \(n\).

My current finding is a complete analytic description of the triangle in terms of a single free parameter \(r\) (the incircle radius).  
With \(BD=F_n=x_0,\;CD=F_{n+1}=u,\;BC=a=x_0+u\) and incircle centre \(I=(x_0,r)\),

\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2x_0r}{x_0^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= -\frac{2ur}{u^{2}-r^{2}} .
\]

Thus  

\[
A=\Bigl(-\frac{m_{AC}a}{m_{AB}-m_{AC}},\;m_{AB}\! \cdot\! \bigl(-\frac{m_{AC}a}{m_{AB}-m_{AC}}\bigr)\Bigr),
\]

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{x_0+m_{AB}r}{1+m_{AB}^{2}},\;m_{AB}\frac{x_0+m_{AB}r}{1+m_{AB}^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a+\frac{(x_0-a)+mr}{1+m^{2}},\;m\frac{(x_0-a)+mr}{1+m^{2}}\Bigr)
\]

with \(m=m_{AC}\).  

All subsequent points (\(K,K',N,T\)) and the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) can be expressed solely as functions of \(r\); the triangle family therefore has exactly one degree of freedom, which will be fixed by that cyclicity equation. This reduction isolates the only variable affecting the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

As \(n\) grows this maximal ratio rapidly converges to \(\alpha\approx2.6180339887\), which equals \(\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}= \frac32+\sqrt{\frac54}\). Thus \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=\frac32,\;q=\frac54\). This contradicts the earlier claim that \(p=1,\;q=3\).

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{\,n+2}}{F_{\,n-1}} .
\]

Numerically, for \(n=2,4,6,8,10\) this gives \(3,\;4,\;21/5,\;55/13,\;144/34\) respectively, matching the computed values. Consequently  

\[

\]

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{p}}\big\rfloor =2^{5^{2}}=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\equiv 57\,447\pmod{99\,991}.
\]
